comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C2, C3, C27, C32, C53. Both evaluations affirm that retinal adaptation begins at the dimmest detectable backgrounds (~0.02 R*/rod/s) matching human behavioral thresholds (~0.01 R*/rod/s). Reviewers found this work 'exciting' with 'high potential significance.'

Both address claims C20, C21, C22 regarding detection thresholds and inhibitory inputs. OpenEval finds the experimental data in Figure 2 fully supportive. Peer reviewers do not dispute the findings but critique the presentation as 'lacking in precise language' and request quantification rather than qualitative descriptions like 'Inhibitory synaptic inputs were small.'

Both address claims C26, C28, C29, C30 regarding Weber law behavior and noise suppression. OpenEval finds Figure 3 data clearly supportive. Peer reviewers do not explicitly challenge findings but raise concerns about multiple gain measures and request clearer explanation of how 'gain changes in the circuit affect both signal and noise.'

Perfect agreement on claims C43-C48 regarding spatial adaptation experiments. Both evaluations affirm that adaptation requires integration over hundreds of rods (~500) and localize the mechanism to the AII amacrine cell level based on receptive field measurements and anatomical constraints.

Strong agreement on claims C49-C52 regarding pathway-specific adaptation and anatomical localization. Both evaluations accept that rod backgrounds do not affect cone-mediated gain and that this, combined with convergence requirements, localizes adaptation to the AII amacrine cell level. Peer result R7 also includes C62 which overlaps with this conclusion.

Agreement on claims C38, C39 regarding rapid adaptation kinetics. Both evaluations affirm that adaptation occurs rapidly (time constants ~0.3 s) at the AII amacrine cell level, with OpenEval citing Figure 5 data and peer reviewers explicitly stating 'Adaptation occurs rapidly.'

Strong agreement on claims C66-C70 regarding hierarchical organization of gain control mechanisms. OpenEval finds the integration of current findings with prior work appropriate. Peer reviewers' enthusiasm ('exciting,' 'high potential significance') and acceptance of specific findings suggest they accept this broader framework, though they request better presentation.

Both address spatial integration calculations (C40, C41, C42 shared). OpenEval finds the mathematical calculation sound. Peer result R2 affirms the broader conclusion that 'as few as 1 or 2 photons are absorbed within a collection of several hundred rods,' which encompasses these calculations. Peer R2 also includes C4, C33, C35, C75.

Partial overlap on claims C71, C72 regarding multiple mechanisms and smooth gain function. OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN due to speculative evolutionary interpretation in C73 lacking evidence. Peer reviewers accept the broader framework about multiple mechanisms without explicitly addressing the evolutionary speculation.

Minimal overlap (C35 only) regarding fluctuating background experiments. OpenEval finds Figure 4 data directly supportive that variance alone does not produce gain changes. Peer result R2 broadly affirms adaptation findings including single-photon sensitivity, which is consistent with but does not specifically address the variance manipulation.

Minimal overlap (C53 only) regarding comparison to behavioral measurements. Both evaluations support the correspondence between retinal measurements (~0.02 R*/rod/s) and human behavioral thresholds (~0.01 R*/rod/s). OpenEval R9 additionally addresses noise sources (C54, C55) not covered in peer R1.

Minimal overlap (C62 only) regarding localization to AII amacrine cells. Both evaluations support this conclusion based on combining multiple experimental constraints. OpenEval R11 also addresses C63, C64 about rod bipolar pathway anatomy and additional data not shown.

Minimal overlap (C75 only) regarding gain control sensitivity. Both evaluations support findings about adaptation at single-photon levels. OpenEval R14 additionally addresses modeling calculations (C76-C79) and functional interpretation (C80-C82) not specifically covered in peer R2.

OpenEval R10 addresses claims C59, C60 regarding limited Rose-deVries behavior and post-retinal contributions to behavioral thresholds. No corresponding peer review evaluation found that specifically addresses these claims about the discrepancy between retinal and behavioral measurements.

OpenEval R15 addresses claims C80-C82 providing functional interpretation of why gain control operates at such low backgrounds relative to rod noise. No corresponding peer review evaluation found that specifically addresses this functional framework and synthesis with rod noise measurements.
